messages.subject: Inconsistent mean and sd in CMR models from JAGS compared to winbugs and nimble
messages.subject_clean: Inconsistent mean and sd in CMR models from JAGS compared to winbugs and nimble
messages.body_plain:
I compared the results of a simple Capture-mark-recapture model using an m-array from Jags, Winbugs and nimble.
Surprisingly, Jags gave different mean results and wider sd than nimble and Winbugs which gave similar results.
The 95% credible interval sin JAGS are thus very large. For instance for the probability of recapture:
  jags gave 0.20-0.93 compared to the others program: 0.53-0.64. The conclusions from JAGS can thus be really different form the other program.
Would anyone have an idea about the causes of these differences?
  Thanks
Floriane

Reproducible example:

# Capture-recapture data (in m-array format, from years 1 to 10)
m <- matrix(c(11,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  70,
              0, 12,  0,  1,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  52,
              0,  0, 15,  5,  1,  0,  0,  0,  0,  42,
              0,  0,  0,  8,  3,  0,  0,  0,  0,  51,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  4,  3,  0,  0,  0,  61,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 12,  2,  3,  0,  66,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 16,  5,  0,  44,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 12,  0,  46,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 11,  71,
              10,  2,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  13,
              0,  7,  0,  1,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  27,
              0,  0, 13,  2,  1,  1,  0,  0,  0,  14,
              0,  0,  0, 12,  2,  0,  0,  0,  0,  20,
              0,  0,  0,  0, 10,  2,  0,  0,  0,  21,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 11,  2,  1,  1,  14,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 12,  0,  0,  18,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 11,  1,  21,
              0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0, 10,  26), ncol = 10, byrow = TRUE)

sink("ipmn.jags")
cat("
    model {
    # Survival and recapture probabilities, as well as productivity
    for (t in 1:(nyears-1)){
    sjuv[t] <- mean.sjuv
    sad[t] <- mean.sad
    p[t] <- mean.p
    }

    mean.sjuv ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.sad ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)

    # 3.2 Likelihood for capture-recapture data: CJS model (2 age classes)
    # Multinomial likelihood
    for (t in 1:2*(nyears-1)){
    m[t,1:nyears] ~ dmulti(pr[t,1:nyears], r[t])
    }

    # m-array cell probabilities for juveniles
    for (t in 1:(nyears-1)){
    # Main diagonal
    q[t] <- 1-p[t]
    pr[t,t] <- sjuv[t] * p[t]
    # Above main diagonal
    for (j in (t+1):(nyears-1)){
    pr[t,j] <- sjuv[t]*prod(sad[(t+1):j])*prod(q[t:(j-1)])*p[j]
    } #j
    # Below main diagonal
    for (j in 1:(t-1)){
    pr[t,j] <- 0
    } #j
    # Last column: probability of non-recapture
    pr[t,nyears] <- 1-sum(pr[t,1:(nyears-1)])
    } #t

    # m-array cell probabilities for adults
    for (t in 1:(nyears-1)){
    # Main diagonal
    pr[t+nyears-1,t] <- sad[t] * p[t]
    # Above main diagonal
    for (j in (t+1):(nyears-1)){
    pr[t+nyears-1,j] <- prod(sad[t:j])*prod(q[t:(j-1)])*p[j]
    } #j
    # Below main diagonal
    for (j in 1:(t-1)){
    pr[t+nyears-1,j] <- 0
    } #j
    # Last column
    pr[t+nyears-1,nyears] <- 1 - sum(pr[t+nyears-1,1:(nyears-1)])
    } #t

    }
    ",fill = TRUE)
sink()

jags.data <- list(m = m, nyears = dim(m)[2], r = rowSums(m))
inits <- list(mean.sjuv = 0.5, mean.sad = 0.5, mean.p = 0.5)
parameters <- c("mean.sjuv", "mean.sad", "mean.p")
library(jagsUI)
ipm <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "ipmn.jags", n.chains = 3, n.thin = 6, n.iter = 2000, n.burnin = 500)
print(ipm, digits = 3)
# mean    sd  2.5%   50%  97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
# mean.sjuv 0.334 0.168 0.122 0.292  0.764    FALSE 1 1.015   137
# mean.sad  0.604 0.215 0.232 0.607  0.976    FALSE 1 1.015   134
# mean.p    0.502 0.204 0.200 0.456  0.930    FALSE 1 1.016   118
# deviance  9.974 2.009 8.005 9.329 15.306    FALSE 1 1.014   279

library(R2WinBUGS)
ipm <- bugs(jags.data, inits, parameters, "ipmn.jags", n.chains = 3, n.thin = 6, n.iter = 2000, n.burnin = 500, debug = F)
print(ipm, digits = 3)
# Inference for Bugs model at "ipmn.jags", fit using WinBUGS,
# 3 chains, each with 2000 iterations (first 500 discarded), n.thin = 6
# n.sims = 750 iterations saved
# mean    sd    2.5%     25%     50%     75%   97.5%  Rhat n.eff
# mean.sjuv   0.269 0.024   0.227   0.251   0.268   0.285   0.321 0.999   750
# mean.sad    0.526 0.030   0.467   0.505   0.526   0.547   0.585 1.016   130
# mean.p      0.610 0.040   0.529   0.584   0.611   0.637   0.688 0.999   750
# deviance  197.661 2.387 194.900 196.000 197.000 198.800 203.927 1.000   750
#
# For each parameter, n.eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
# and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor (at convergence, Rhat=1).
#
# DIC info (using the rule, pD = Dbar-Dhat)
# pD = 3.0 and DIC = 200.6
# DIC is an estimate of expected predictive error (lower deviance is better).

library(nimble)
codejags<-readBUGSmodel('ipmn.jags',data=jags.data,inits=inits)
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(codejags)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(codejags)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = codejags)
Cmcmc$run(10000)
samples <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)[2000:10000,]
apply(samples, 2, mean)
# mean.p  mean.sad mean.sjuv
# 0.6078309 0.5273773 0.2692511
apply(samples, 2, sd)
# mean.p   mean.sad  mean.sjuv
# 0.03982141 0.02839809 0.02488084

messages.body_plain:
Without looking closely at your code, one of the first places I might look when troubleshooting is the initial values. I know that JAGS has different requirements for initial values than WinBUGS, at least for occupancy models and N-mixture models. Sometimes they can have a big influence on how well the model performs.

Hello,

I have only tentative/partial understanding of how to structure jags model code (the AHM book Vol. 1 has been a great help recently, thank you).  I am modeling 36 tree species distributions (presence-absence) across two time periods with covariates that are drawn from a common distribution.  Time is included in the model as a categorical covariate.  Site locations are not the same across the two time periods but are independent samples within/across the same study area.

My model code below works well to assess differences in each species' distribution across the two time periods.  However, I would like to assess whether there is an overall/aggregate difference in distributions between the two time periods, across all species (I hope this makes sense; would be glad to try to clarify what I am asking if needed).  I need help understanding how to add code to the model for this purpose.

I have tried several approaches that generate syntax errors or compilation errors such as "Attempt to redefine node p[1]".  (I have also tried completely restructuring my code, along with my input data, based on examples in the AHM book, but have not yet figured out how to do this for my particular model needs.)

Below is the model code I have used to date (before reading the AHM book; not elegant, but does work; uses R2jags).  Covariates are time (categorical; the model is intended to compare species distributions across two time periods), elevation, elevation squared, a topographic index (lfi), and several interactions between these covariates.  There are no replicate observations at individual sites, so there is no observation model in that sense.  The model lets jags determine initial values.  Any help you can provide would be much appreciated!

mod.sp<- function () {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    presence[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
    logit(p[i]) <- B.sp[sp[i]]*int[i] + B.sp.time[sp[i]]*time[i] + B.sp.elev[sp[i]]*elev[i] + B.sp.elev2[sp[i]]*elevsq[i] + B.sp.lfi[sp[i]]*lfi[i] + B.sp.elev.lfi[sp[i]]*elev[i]*lfi[i] + B.sp.lfi.time[sp[i]]*lfi[i]*time[i] + B.sp.elev.time[sp[i]]*elev[i]*time[i] + B.sp.elev2.time[sp[i]]*elevsq[i]*time[i] + B.sp.elev2.lfi[sp[i]]*elevsq[i]*lfi[i]
  }
  for (j in 1:S) {
    B.sp[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp)
    B.sp.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.time)
    B.sp.elev[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev)
    B.sp.elev2[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev2)
    B.sp.lfi[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.lfi)
    B.sp.elev.lfi[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev.lfi)
    B.sp.lfi.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.lfi.time)
    B.sp.elev.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev.time)
    B.sp.elev2.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev2.time)
    B.sp.elev2.lfi[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev2.lfi)
  }

  tau.sp<-pow(sigma.sp, -2)
  sigma.sp~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.time<-pow(sigma.sp.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev<-pow(sigma.sp.elev, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev2<-pow(sigma.sp.elev2, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev2~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.lfi<-pow(sigma.sp.lfi, -2)
  sigma.sp.lfi~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev.lfi<-pow(sigma.sp.elev.lfi, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev.lfi~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.lfi.time<-pow(sigma.sp.lfi.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.lfi.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev.time<-pow(sigma.sp.elev.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev2.time<-pow(sigma.sp.elev2.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev2.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev2.lfi<-pow(sigma.sp.elev2.lfi, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev2.lfi~dunif(0,10000)
}

out.sp.fullmod <- jags(data=data.sp, parameters.to.save=par.sp, n.chains=3, n.iter=30000, n.burnin=1000, model.file=mod.sp)

This might be overly simplistic and someone else on the list might have a better answer. However, one approach that comes to mind to assess "the overall difference in distributions between time periods across all species" would be to evaluate a non-species-specific version of B.sp.time. Let's call the new global variable B.time; it will not be indexed by species. You might create a model that includes the term B.time * time. You could keep the other variables indexed by species if you wish, but I don't think you could include both B.sp.time and B.time in the same model. However, in this case, the estimate of B.time would be affected by the sample sizes. If you have much more data for some species than others, the value of B.time would be strongly influenced by those species. (I'm not sure why time is given as time[i] in your model - is the i index for species? Does the time period of interest differ among species? If so, this might not be the right approach.)

Another option might be to keep your model as written, and then take the mean of B.sp.time. You could assign that to a new variable, like "B.mean.time <- mean(B.sp.time)" (somewhere in your model code, outside of the "for i in 1:N" loop), and then add B.mean.time to your par.sp list to record the estimate in the model output. You could likewise record sd(B.sp.time) or anything else of interest. This wouldn't have the biases resulting from uneven sample sizes, but maybe this wouldn't fully capture the nuances of the overall change between time periods.

Like I said, either option might be too simple to capture what you want to measure, but just a couple of thoughts.

Cheers,

Emily

Andre,

I’ve run lots of occupancy models in jags, and the thing is if there is a 1 in the initial values where there isn’t a 1 in the data, you will get that error every time. Basically, your initial values should match your detection data or it won’t work. For example, if y[i, ] = 0  1  0, the initial z value should be 1 but if y[i, ] = 0  0  0 the initial value has to be 0.

It works the same as you start aggregating up. WinBUGS doesn’t have this issue.

Incidentally, it’s the same with N-mixture models where the initial values need to match the counts.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Andre, Andrew, Peter, et al.

Andrew: I think you meant the other way round: if you initialize a z at 0 when there is a 1 in the data for the same time point, then this represents a contradiction between model, data and inits and JAGS will crash (it wouldn't be a contradiction in a model that allows false positives).

Normally you can initialize the z's for standard occupancy models (i.e., with false-negatives only) with 1's for everybody and that should work. Have you tried that, Andre ? Although you have an autologistic model and perhaps that makes things more difficult?

Perhaps you can run the model in WinBUGS for a couple 100 iterations and then take the estimates from that as inits for another run in JAGS ? Or: if the model runs in good old WinBUGS, avoid JAGS altogether ?

Best regards  ---- Marc

PS: And I have no clue for why JAGS is so picky with its inits. For some more complicated models this pickiness may make JAGS almost useless, because you may be unable to get any set of inits that avoids such data/model/inits contradictions.

To: Peter Solymos; luza....@gmail.com
Cc: hmec...@googlegroups.com
Subject: RE: Problems with initial values in JAGS but not in WinBUGS

Andre,

I’ve run lots of occupancy models in jags, and the thing is if there is a 1 in the initial values where there isn’t a 1 in the data, you will get that error every time. Basically, your initial values should match your detection data or it won’t work. For example, if y[i, ] = 0  1  0, the initial z value should be 1 but if y[i, ] = 0  0  0 the initial value has to be 0.

It works the same as you start aggregating up. WinBUGS doesn’t have this issue.

Incidentally, it’s the same with N-mixture models where the initial values need to match the counts.

Andrew D. Crosby

Subject: Re: Problems with initial values in JAGS but not in WinBUGS

André,

Have you tried setting all values in z to 1? If I understand correctly, z is your latent state matrix. JAGS can be quite picky about those if initial values of the hyper parameters (flat priors I assume) do not lead to probabilities that are in line with the values in z.

HTH,

Peter

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

One more idea of how to initialize the z vector/matrix in jags is to initialize it as 1 for all sites where the species was detected, and set to NA for all other sites:

z <- ifelse(y > 0, 1, NA)  # (in this example, the surveys are aggregated into binomial data)

I then include the z vector/matrix as one of the data inputs:
jags_data <-  list("y", "z", ...)

Cheers,
Kristin
